smells.finding: The 'coerce an Optional[Path] to Optional[str] for build_crew_argv' expression `str(x) if x is not None else None` is written three times (CliBackend.dispatch, CliBackend.resume, and the handoff-path resolution), and the nullable-handoff guard is expressed four times in four shapes: CrewSpec.__post_init__ ('a crew needs a job'), build_crew_argv's else-raise, main()'s `missing` list, and main()'s explicit handoff/spine check. Minor and each site is defensible on its own (the docstring calls the build_crew_argv one 'a second, cheaper backstop'), but four spellings of one rule is where they drift apart. Observation, not a blocker.

(handoff, spine) travel together through build_crew_argv, CrewSpec, build_entry and launch_crew, which is the shape of a clump -- but CrewSpec is already the parameter object for exactly this tuple, so the clump is named, not loose.

The hook is a Python PROGRAM carried as a raw str constant (_WAIVE_HOOK_PY), embedded in a shell string, embedded in a JSON string. Three levels of stringly-typed nesting, guarded by one bare `assert` on one interpolated value. This is the direct cause of r4f: the type system cannot help, so quoting correctness rests on a runtime assertion that python -O strips. The repo already ships a typed-ish answer (install_constellation.py::build_hook_command + assert_shell_safe_command, which builds a hook command from a resolved interpreter and a script PATH rather than an inline program). Raised as a blocker under r4f, not merely as a smell.
build_crew_argv now takes launcher plus five keyword-only params (role, handoff, model, session, spine); launch_crew takes eleven.

override.repo_standard: scripts/run_crew.py's established convention: keyword-only parameters at every dispatch seam, with CrewSpec as the parameter object where a spec is constructed.
override.reason: Every added parameter is keyword-only, so no call site can transpose arguments, and the one place the list would genuinely be unwieldy already has its parameter object (CrewSpec). build_crew_argv is deliberately PURE so tests can assert argv without spawning; threading a spec into it would couple the pure function to the dataclass it exists to be testable apart from.

smells.finding: Making one field nullable required coordinated edits at eight sites: CrewSpec.handoff, CrewSpec.__post_init__, build_entry, build_crew_argv, CliBackend.dispatch, CliBackend.resume, ExternalBackend.dispatch, launch_crew, and main()'s argument checks. The change made all of them -- but it did NOT make the ninth, CrewBackend.verify / main()'s required --result, which is precisely the site r4g fails on. That is the diagnostic value of this smell here: a change that has to touch nine places will miss one, and it did.

scripts/run_crew.py now changes for three unrelated reasons: how a crew is IDENTIFIED and recorded (registry, session names, recovery), what a crew is TOLD to do (prompt construction), and what a crew is PERMITTED to do (allowed tools, and now an inline settings/hook policy). The permission-policy concern is new with this change and is the least related of the three -- WAIVE_DENY_REASON, _WAIVE_HOOK_PY and crew_settings_json are a security policy that happens to live in a launcher. Observation for a future seam (a crew_policy module), explicitly not a blocker for this bounded change.

The nullable handoff, the spine branch and the hook are each driven by a named requirement in the handoff; nothing was built for a hypothetical caller. The `spine` parameter defaults to None, which keeps every existing call site untouched -- backward compatibility, not speculation.

The diff is comment-heavy even by this file's standards: a 9-line comment above CREW_ALLOWED_TOOLS explaining why it is hand-typed, an 11-line comment above WAIVE_DENY_REASON, a 6-line comment above _WAIVE_HOOK_PY, and inline comments at each refusal site. Several explain a workaround rather than a design (the hand-typed grant, the single-quote hazard).
